blocks.prompt: 2 (i) [printed as i)] Find the rank of the following matrix: \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -6 & 1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\)
blocks.explanation:
A rank question: rank = number of non-zero rows in echelon form.
We must find one number.
Plan: make leading 1s column by column with zeros below them, push zero rows to the bottom, then count.
steps:
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -6 & 1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\), a \(3 \times 4\) matrix.
To find: rank of \(A\).
Method: Reduce \(A\) to echelon form by row operations; the rank is the number of non-zero rows.

Leading 1 in row 2
By \(\left(-\frac{1}{8}\right)R_2 \to R_2'\)
\(R_2'\): \(0\), \(1\), \(-\frac{7}{8}\), \(-\frac{1}{8}\)
\[\sim \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{7}{8} & -\frac{1}{8} \\ 0 & 4 & -5 & -5\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Dividing \(R_2\) by \(-8\) makes its first non-zero entry 1.

Leading 1 in row 3
By \(\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)R_3 \to R_3'\)
\(R_3'\): \(0\), \(0\), \(1\), \(3\)
\[\sim \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{7}{8} & -\frac{1}{8} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Multiplying \(R_3\) by \(-\frac{2}{3}\) makes \(-\frac{3}{2}\) equal to 1. The matrix is now in echelon form.

Count the non-zero rows
The echelon form has 3 non-zero rows.
\[\text{Rank of } A = 3\]
Why: By definition, rank = number of non-zero rows in echelon form. (A \(3 \times 4\) matrix can have rank at most 3.)

blocks.prompt: 2 (ii) Find the rank of the following matrix: \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & 6 \\ -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\)
blocks.explanation:
A rank question: rank = number of non-zero rows in echelon form.
We must find one number.
Plan: make leading 1s column by column with zeros below them, push zero rows to the bottom, then count.
steps:
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & 6 \\ -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\), a \(4 \times 3\) matrix.
To find: rank of \(A\).
Method: Reduce \(A\) to echelon form by row operations; the rank is the number of non-zero rows.

Move the zero row to the bottom
By \(R_2 \leftrightarrow R_4\)
\[\sim \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: In echelon form zero rows stay at the bottom; \(R_4\) also has a ready leading 1.

Leading 1 in row 3
By \(\frac{1}{3}R_3 \to R_3'\)
\(R_3'\): \(0\), \(0\), \(1\)
\[\sim \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Dividing by 3. The matrix is now in echelon form.

Count the non-zero rows
The echelon form has 3 non-zero rows.
\[\text{Rank of } A = 3\]
Why: By definition, rank = number of non-zero rows in echelon form. (A \(4 \times 3\) matrix can have rank at most 3.)

blocks.prompt: 2 (iii) Find the rank of the following matrix: \(\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 & -3 & -2 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & -2 & -3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\)
blocks.explanation:
A rank question: rank = number of non-zero rows in echelon form.
We must find one number.
Plan: make leading 1s column by column with zeros below them, push zero rows to the bottom, then count.
steps:
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 & -3 & -2 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & -2 & -3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\), a \(4 \times 5\) matrix.
To find: rank of \(A\).
Method: Reduce \(A\) to echelon form by row operations; the rank is the number of non-zero rows.

Bring a 1 to the top of column 1
By \(R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2\)
\[\sim \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & -3 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & -2 & -3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: \(R_2\) starts with 1, which avoids fractions.

Bring a 1 into the pivot of row 2
By \(R_2 \leftrightarrow R_4\)
\[\sim \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & -3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 & 7 \\ 0 & -1 & 6 & 8 & 5 \\ 0 & -7 & 6 & 9 & 7\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: \(R_4\) has 1 in column 2, again avoiding fractions.

Clear column 3 below the pivot
By \(R_4 + (-1)R_3 \to R_4'\)
\(R_4'\): \(0 + 0 = 0\), \(0 + 0 = 0\), \(6 - 6 = 0\), \(30 - 11 = 19\), \(56 - 12 = 44\)
\[\sim \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & -3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 & 11 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 19 & 44\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Rows 3 and 4 both start with 6 in column 3, so subtracting removes it.

Count the non-zero rows
The echelon form has 4 non-zero rows.
\[\text{Rank of } A = 4\]
Why: By definition, rank = number of non-zero rows in echelon form. (A \(4 \times 5\) matrix can have rank at most 4.)
